extracted.intended_audience: trial and appellate patent litigators, district court judges, and expert witnesses in patent damages cases
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and procedural standards for admitting (and reviewing the admission of) a damages expert's testimony in a patent infringement case, focusing on Rule 702/Daubert, reliance on prior licenses and fact witness testimony, and harmless-error/new-trial analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 702(b) — based on sufficient facts or data
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony must be “based on sufficient facts or data” (FED. R. EVID. 702(b)); the court examines the facts or data on which the expert purports to rely—not the record as a whole—to determine sufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An expert’s relied-upon facts/data must themselves constitute a sufficient basis for the opinion. The court should not treat extraneous record evidence that the expert did not rely upon as curing a deficient basis. If an expert's opinion depends on facts/data not actually before or relied upon by the expert, Rule 702(b) may not be satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability requirement under Rule 702/Daubert
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 702 sets an overarching requirement of reliability for expert testimony; the sufficiency of an expert’s factual basis must be tied to the ultimate reliability of the opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should apply Daubert sensibilities—methodology and factual basis must support reliable opinion. Mere ipse dixit (unsupported assertion) does not make an expert opinion reliable (citing Joiner). The advisory committee note recognizes the gatekeeping role but also that reliability is a lower threshold than correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court’s gatekeeping role and standard of review
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts have broad discretion as gatekeepers in admitting expert testimony; appellate review is for abuse of discretion and should only find error when the ruling is manifestly erroneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because determinations are often fact-intensive, appellate courts should defer to district courts unless there is a clear abuse. The gatekeeping role is not intended to replace the adversary system; credibility and weight are for the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of expert’s reliance on prior licenses to establish a per-unit royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert relying on prior license agreements to establish an existing per-unit royalty rate must show that the licenses actually support the asserted rate—the mere presence of lump-sum licenses or unilateral recital language is insufficient if untethered to evidence that parties agreed to a per-unit rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must assess whether license terms legally bind parties to a per-unit rate versus merely stating a lump-sum. Unilateral 'whereas' recitals or boilerplate that do not reflect mutual agreement or calculations tied to sales figures may be an inadequate basis. Experts cannot convert lump sums into unit rates without evidentiary support (e.g., underlying sales/projections or a clear contractual calculation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fact witness (personal knowledge) testimony to support expert opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: A fact witness’s testimony based on personal knowledge (FED. R. EVID. 602) may provide a proper basis for an expert’s opinion if the expert actually relies on it and the testimony was properly admitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the fact witness’s testimony was before the jury without objection, an expert may rely on it; however, if the fact testimony was expressly excluded at trial, the expert may not rely on it. Parties must object timely under Rule 103 to preserve challenges to introduction of fact testimony or to its use by experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on relying on assertions about advisors’ confidential sales data
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert’s claim that advisors had access to licensees’ confidential sales data (and used that to compute lump sums) cannot be accepted absent record evidence those advisors actually had such access and performed such calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is no record evidence that advisors accessed sales data or performed calculations, district courts can exclude testimony asserting reliance on such advisors. Arguments relying on supposed but unproven advisor analyses amount to unsupported assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible use of market share data as a check on damages calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Undisputed market share data can be used by an expert as a reasonableness check or to estimate licensees’ sales (and thereby test whether lump sums correspond to a particular per-unit rate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Market share evidence may reasonably allow an expert or jury to infer relative sales and to assess whether lump sums comport with an asserted per-unit rate, provided the market-share evidence itself is reliable and actually relied upon by the expert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract interpretation and apportionment considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a license legally binds the contracting parties to a per-unit royalty rate (as opposed to only a lump-sum) may implicate contract interpretation—typically a question of law subject to de novo review on appeal—and apportionment issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the issue is one of contract interpretation, appellate courts may review de novo. But parties must be given notice/opportunity to brief contract-law issues; courts should not sua sponte transform a Rule 702 admissibility dispute into a contract-law appeal without fair notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of exclusionary remedy for flawed expert analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: If only a discrete subset of an expert’s analyses (e.g., a single Georgia‑Pacific factor) is flawed, wholesale exclusion of all of the expert’s testimony may be disproportionate absent explanation showing that the flaw undermines the remainder of the opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should consider whether other admissible portions of the expert’s methodology and evidence can support parts of the opinion. The remedy for an admissibility error should be tailored to the defect; blanket exclusion requires justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmless-error / prejudicial-effect standard for new-trial motions
rubrics_metrics.description: A party seeking a new trial based on erroneously admitted evidence must show the error was prejudicial—that it affected substantial rights and influenced the jury or had more than a very slight effect on the verdict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Fifth Circuit precedent, duplicative admission of evidence that is also properly before the jury is unlikely to be deemed prejudicial. The moving party bears the burden to demonstrate that the erroneously admitted evidence materially affected the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of objections under Rule 103
rubrics_metrics.description: To preserve appellate review of evidentiary error (including testimony that should have been excluded), a party must timely make the proper objection at trial under FED. R. EVID. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to object to testimony (e.g., a fact witness’s statements about how a lump sum was derived) forfeits certain appellate challenges. Parties that do not object at trial cannot later rely on those objections on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert must actually rely on the evidence it cites in support
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 702 requires the expert’s relied-upon facts or data to be the basis for the testimony; courts examine whether the expert actually used or relied upon the record evidence claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An expert cannot be saved by alternative record evidence that the expert did not rely upon in forming the opinion; admissibility turns on the expert’s actual basis, as reflected in the report/testimony. If the expert used certain data only as an after-the-fact 'check' (or did not use it at all), courts evaluate whether that reliance suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury’s role in weighing credibility and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Credibility determinations and the weight to be given testimony are for the jury—not the court’s gatekeeping function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gatekeeping should exclude unreliable expert methodologies or baseless factual premises, but should not supplant the jury’s role in choosing between competing versions of facts when both are properly in evidence.
